title: Call for papers – Collections Across Borders conference, Mexico, 13-16 April 2027
content:
The IFLA Rare Books and Special Collections section is now welcoming papers for Collections Across Borders: Provenance, Circulation and Dispersal of Documentary Heritage; a conference to be held in Mexico City and Puebla, 13-16 April 2027. We invite librarians, researchers, archivists, curators, conservators, antiquarian booksellers, and heritage professionals to explore the provenance, circulation and dispersal of documentary heritage.

Books, manuscrips, archives, and historical collections have corssed borders through trade, collecting, donation, inheritance, and confiscation. These movements have shaped and dispersed collection, creating new relationships between institutions, communities, and cultural traditions. Provenance research reconstructs these histories through material and documentary evidence, connecting individual objects to broader historical contexts while raising questions about cultural heritage, memory, access, and institutional responsibility.

Contributions may address, but are not limited to, the following themes:

  • Provenance research and the material history of collections
  • Circulation, collecting, and dispersal of documentary heritage

title: Show your library’s impact! Use the new IFLA Storytelling Manual to put your work on the map
content:
Has your library helped address a challenge in your community? Have its activities made a difference in people’s lives? If so, that is a story worth telling, you just need to bring it to life.  

IFLA presents the fully revised edition of Libraries and the Sustainable Development Goals: A Storytelling Manual, a practical resource to help librarians and library advocates develop, write and share compelling stories about their projects and their contributions to sustainable development.

Every library has a story worth telling – events, workshops, community meetings, language clubs, collaborations are all ways libraries contribute to improving lives of the communities they serve. And by helping people access information, gain knowledge, develop skills and connect with opportunities, libraries advance sustainable development every day.

Yet these contributions are not always visible or recognised by decision-makers and other stakeholders. Stories backed up by evidence can help change that, showing the difference libraries make in a clear manner to those who can support and strengthen their work.

title: IFLA Volunteer Model Review: Sharing Survey Results
content:
The result from three surveys run in the context of IFLA’s volunteer model review, itself part of IFLA’s Sustainable Futures Journey, shed helpful light on the experience of volunteers, their employers and our members. They underline strong points, but also areas for improvement.

IFLA’s Sustainable Futures Journey is a set of steps that IFLA’s Governing Board has launched with the goal of ensuring that our Federation is in the best possible shape to continue to deliver on its strategy and missions into its second century.

A major part of this is the review of our volunteering model, which is the driver of so much of what we do. In order to meet the expectations of volutneers current and future, their employers, our members, our partners, and the wider library field, we need to make sure that we have a model that delivers.

As a first step in this process, we have run a series of surveys, alongside focus groups and informal conversations, targeting different groups of identified stakeholders. We are very grateful to all those who took the time to respond, and are happy now to share the results.

title: Behind the Counter: What a National Survey Reveals About Public Library Staff in Spain
content:
A new report published by Spain’s Ministry of Culture looks closely at the people who keep the country’s libraries running. La realidad profesional del personal de las bibliotecas de titularidad pública en España (“The professional reality of staff in publicly owned libraries in Spain”) was prepared by the Professional Development Working Group of the Spanish Library Cooperation Council (Consejo de Cooperación Bibliotecaria).

The study was led by Carlos Miguel Tejada Artigas (Universidad Complutense de Madrid). It is based on a nationwide survey answered by 2,604 professionals working in all types of publicly owned libraries. Public libraries make up the largest group: 45.4% of respondents work in municipal libraries and a further 4.4% in regional public libraries. Because results are broken down by library type, the study shows clearly where public libraries resemble the rest of the system and where they stand apart.

title: Towards the futures we want: IFLA comes to Mexico City
content:
IFLA will reach a key milestone in our progress towards our centennial Congress with a set of events in Mexico City in April 2027.

What can we be doing today to maximise the chances of achieving the future we want for libraries and knowledge, and what even is this future? And what does this mean for how we approach key international frameworks such as the post-2030 Agenda?

These will be the key questions in focus when IFLA’s Governing Board comes to Mexico City on 26-29 April 2027.

The National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) has kindly agreed to host a series of events in addition to the Board meetings, making it possible to engage with the Mexican and wider Latin American and Caribbean library communities, check in on all of the discussions taking place as part of IFLA100, and look ahead both to IFLA’s 2027 Congress and the SDG Summit that will kick-start the preparation of what comes after the UN’s 2030 Agenda and its Sustainable Development Goals.

In addition to meetings of the Board itself, we are planning on events for the wider field, drawing on expertise from inside and outside the field, designed around engagement and conversation with colleagues.

title: Join the IFLA Library History SIG | Call for Expression of Interest – Election 2027
content:
Get involved in the IFLA 2027 Elections! Make sure to submit your nominations before the December 9 deadline. For full details and instructions, please consult the IFLA announcement: Elections 2027 – Call for Expressions of Interest.

If you are passionate about library history, we warmly invite you to join the LIBHIST SIG projects and events as we celebrate the IFLA Centenary year.

Our Special Interest Group is currently undergoing a phase of transformation, and we will continue to curate both the history and the future of our profession. We will be delighted to welcome colleagues with expertise in history who are motivated to shape the future. Join us!

title: IFLA Regional Offices 2027-2029: Hosts announced
content:
At its most recent formal meeting, IFLA’s Governing Board took its decision about the hosts of IFLA’s Regional Offices for Asia-Oceania, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East and North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa for 2027-2029.

IFLA’s Regional Offices are hosted by institutions committed to enabling the full participation of libraries and library and information workers in their region in the work of IFLA. They have an important role both in helping colleagues around the world benefit from belonging to an international field, as well as ensuring that our Headquarters and wider organisation are aware of key issues and needs. 

They have been a part of IFLA’s operation for many years already, and indeed as part of our work to put more of IFLA’s archives online, you can now dig into some of the back catalogues of newsletters and other work they have done.

Today, in the context of our Sustainable Futures Journey, they not only fulfil their traditional role, but have a mission to be hubs, not only for learning and sharing between professionals, but also for libraries to meet and form links with external partners, including funders.

title: IFLA President’s Message October 2026
content:
This message was shared directly with all IFLA members and volunteers in all IFLA langauges earlier this month.

Dear all,

Another month has passed, and so time for another message sharing an update about what’s been going on at IFLA, and some of the key themes and questions on the agenda.  

It seems that every time I send one of these, I am arriving home from a period of travel. This time is no different – my latest engagement on behalf of IFLA was a great set of events first in Oslo at the National Library Forum hosted by the National Library of Norway where I had the opportunity to meet Åsa Wetås, the recently appointed Director of the National Library and then in South Africa, centred on the 17th Stellenbosch University Library Symposium. The Symposium in Stellenbosch was particularly significant, marking the retirement of a great past IFLA President, Ellen Tise. I was also privileged to join an event organised by our Regional Office team at the University of South Africa. 

It’s been very welcome to see, across these events, how much the global field has embraced IFLA100 – our centenary – as an opportunity to take a moment for celebration and reflection.

title: Futures Club #6: You Can’t Create What You Can’t Imagine
content:
How can libraries help people think about the future? One of the clearest lessons from Futures Club #6, with Thomas Sture Rasmussen and Lotte Hviid Dhyrbye from the Danish Library Association was was that the answer is not to predict what will happen. Instead, libraries can give people the tools, spaces and confidence to explore different possible futures for themselves.

The Association’s work was built on a combination of practical experience, as well as the record of the Library of the Future think-tank. The think tank had started as a form of aggregator, bringing together data and thinkers to prepare reports setting out visions of the future of libraries. However, over time, the emphasis shifted towards how to equip libraries to ask their own questions and imagine their own possibilities.

title: A chance for a comprehensive approach? Knowledge and information in the 2026 Voluntary National Reviews
content:
Governments are recognising the role of knowledge and information in achieving progress across the United Nations’ 2030 Agenda, both as goals in themselves and as an enabler. They also underline the need for specialists, infrastructures, and intermediation. Yet a scattered way of doing things risks missing out on opportunities for a more strategic appraoch, notably one that realises the potential of libraries.

IFLA has released its analysis of the 2026 Voluntary National Reviews (VNRs) of implementation of the SDGs, from the perspective of the contribution made by knowledge and information.

The wealth of references to this serve as a strong indicator of both the strength and richness of this role. While there is unevenness in the number and variety of references from one Review to the next, these are present in every single review.
